extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics and teleology); translators and readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of Kant's Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the evaluative principles and standards Kant (and the editor) set out for aesthetic (judgement of taste, beautiful, sublime) and teleological judgements, plus editorial guidance on translation and study. Intended to capture the criteria used to judge objects, art, and natural purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is aesthetical (§1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant frames judgements of taste as distinct from cognitive judgements — they concern feeling/pleasure rather than knowledge. Treat aesthetic judgement as a faculty-related, non-conceptual evaluative act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction determining the judgement of taste is disinterested
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested (§2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine aesthetic judgement's pleasure must be free from desire to possess or from practical interest; the observer's personal ends must not determine the judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in the pleasant is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the pleasant is bound up with interest (§3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ordinary pleasantness (linked to desire/interest) from purely aesthetic pleasure when evaluating responses to objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction in the good is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the good is bound up with interest (§4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or practical approval (the 'good') entails an interest and cannot be conflated with disinterested aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful gives universal satisfaction apart from concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Beautiful is that which apart from concepts is represented as the object of a universal satisfaction’ (§6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgement that calls something beautiful claims a kind of universal validity despite being based on no determinate concept; when assessing art or nature, test whether the pleasure is claimed as universally communicable rather than conceptually founded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of taste is subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of the satisfaction in a judgement of taste is represented as subjective (§8, §22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant holds that universal assent is expected but is not objective knowledge; when evaluating aesthetic claims, note that the asserted universality rests on a shared sensibility (sensus communis), not on theoretical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of feeling and judgement in taste is investigable
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigation of whether in a judgement of taste the feeling of pleasure precedes or follows judging of the object (§9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of aesthetic responses should consider whether pleasure is antecedent to the judgement or produced by the act of judging — relevant in analyzing 'pure' taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful as purposiveness without definite purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste has nothing at its basis but the form of the purposiveness of an object (or of its mode of representation) — purposiveness without definite purpose (§11, §12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic value depends on perceived formal purposiveness (form harmonising with cognitive faculties) even when no external function or definite purpose can be assigned; assess whether perceived purposiveness is formal rather than teleological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgements rest on a priori grounds (pure judgement of taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste rests on a priori grounds; the pure judgement of taste is independent of charm and emotion (§12, §13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim of pure taste should be evaluated for independence from contingent charms (colour, sentiment) and for its appeal to a priori faculties rather than empirical contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free vs dependent beauty (purity of judgement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure judgement of taste is independent of charm and emotion; a judgement declaring an object beautiful under a definite concept is not pure (e.g., free vs dependent beauty, §13, §16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether art/nature is judged 'beautiful' in Kantian terms, distinguish free beauty (form only) from dependent beauty (bound to concepts or functions). Dependent beauty is not a pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of Beauty and independence from concept of perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is quite independent of the concept of perfection; discussion includes the Ideal of Beauty (§15, §17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate aesthetic value with perfection or fitness; evaluate whether beauty is being judged for formal purposiveness rather than conformity to an ideal perfect standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective necessity and sensus communis underlie aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective necessity we ascribe to a judgement of taste is conditioned by the Idea of a common sense (sensus communis) — necessity represented as objective under that presupposition (§19–§22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that others ought to agree in taste depend on presupposing a shared faculty of judgment. Evaluate appeals to universal agreement by testing whether they invoke a common cognitive ground rather than demonstrable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability of aesthetic feeling and taste as sensus communis
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction and discussion of the communicability of sensation and of taste as a kind of sensus communis (§38–§41).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess aesthetic claims for their communicability: does the judgement invite others to the same feeling by reference to shared faculties? This is central to Kant’s account of why taste claims universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime divided into mathematical and dynamical
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is analysed into the Mathematically Sublime (magnitude) and the Dynamically Sublime (power); the sublime excites a movement in the mind and is rooted in the subject (§24–§29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating experiences called 'sublime', determine whether the response is to magnitude/absoluteness (mathematical) or to might/power that threatens but does not frighten (dynamical); Kant locates sublimity in the subject’s reflection on its own faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime awakens feeling of supersensible destination; links to moral feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling of the sublime awakens a feeling of the supersensible destination of man and is connected with the presupposition of moral feeling (editor’s summary; §29 and later dialectic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant ties the aesthetic experience of the sublime to moral awareness — in assessment, note any claimed moral or transcendent dimension arising from sublime experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art as art of genius; genius gives rule to art
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art is the art of genius: an innate mental disposition through which Nature gives the rule to Art; art differs from science by absence of definite concepts (§43–§50).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works of art by whether they exhibit 'aesthetic Ideas' produced by genius (original, non-conceptual) and whether taste (self-restraint) has regulated genius; artistic method may be incommunicable but must respect canons of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness of nature: formal vs real purposiveness (teleology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective purposiveness of Nature is distinguished between purposiveness merely formal and purposiveness that is material/adapted to ends (§61–§63).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating biological or natural phenomena, distinguish mere formal appearances of purposiveness (fit to our faculties) from claims that things are adapted to definite ends; the latter invites teleological explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised beings as natural purposes; principle for judging internal purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Things regarded as natural purposes are organised beings; in such products every part exists by means of and for the sake of the other parts and the whole (§65–§66).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess living organisms as systems whose parts appear mutually purposive; Kant treats this interdependence as the basis for teleological judgement in biology and as not wholly reducible to mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Teleology and the method of judging nature as a system of purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle of the teleological judging of nature in general as a system of purposes; teleology as internal principle of natural science (§67–§68, Appendix §§79–83).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological judgement as a regulative (reflective) principle for explaining organisms and natural systems, but be aware Kant’s teleology is methodological/regulative — not a constitutive scientific law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technic vs Mechanism; subordination of mechanical to teleological explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between the Technic (teleological operation) of nature and Mechanism; necessary subordination of the mechanical to teleological principle in explaining a natural purpose (Appendix §§80–81).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining natural purposes, consider whether mechanistic accounts suffice or whether teleological (technic-like) explanations are required; Kant allows methodology that pairs mechanism with teleology without dogmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement has antinomies and limits; cannot be dogmatic
rubrics_metrics.description: There are antinomies of the judgement about teleology; the concept of natural purpose is inexplicable dogmatically and teleology is a critical principle for reflective judgement (§69–§76).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat teleological explanations cautiously: they resolve certain explanatory needs but lead to antinomies if treated dogmatically. Evaluate teleological claims with an eye to their regulative, not constitutive, status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proof and limits: use and limitation of the moral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the moral proof of the Being of God, limitation of its validity, and the use of the moral argument (Appendix §§86–91).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant connects teleology, moral reasoning, and belief: when assessing moral-theological arguments, apply Kant’s cautions about scope and evidential limits and distinguish kinds of belief produced by practical faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and editorial guidance: preserve technical terms consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Translator should select English equivalents for German technical terms and retain them consistently; preserving distinctions may require arbitrariness (editor’s note).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For translators and editors: maintain consistent renderings of Kant’s technical vocabulary across the text to preserve distinctions, even if no English word is perfect; document choices and be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study advice: read the ipsissima verba; use aids cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are warned not to rely solely on secondary aids; personal study of the ipsissima verba (the author’s exact words) is necessary for satisfactory knowledge (editor’s introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage direct engagement with the original text rather than summaries; use translations/paraphrases as aids but not substitutes for careful reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic cautions: beware Kant’s technicality and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant’s faults noted include over-technicality and frequent repetition; important points can be obscured by long, laborious style (editor’s introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Kant’s arguments or any translation, be mindful that repetition may mask new points and that dense technical prose may require patient, repeated reading to extract key criteria.
